title: Second-order linear ODEs (homogeneous, undetermined coefficients, superposition)
summary: Constant-coefficient second-order equations are solved from the roots of the characteristic equation (distinct, repeated, complex), and forced equations by undetermined coefficients with the tˢ resonance rule plus superposition. Expect at least one full IVP and one "write the form" question.

lesson.title: Linear second-order equations and their solution space

blocks.text: y″ + p(t)y′ + q(t)y = g(t). With constant coefficients: ay″ + by′ + cy = g(t), a ≠ 0. Homogeneous if g = 0. Write L[y] = ay″ + by′ + cy; L is a linear operator: L[c₁y₁ + c₂y₂] = c₁L[y₁] + c₂L[y₂].

blocks.name: Existence and uniqueness
blocks.text: If p, q, g are continuous on an interval I containing t₀, the initial value problem with y(t₀) = Y₀, y′(t₀) = Y₁ has exactly one solution on I.

blocks.name: The solution space is 2-dimensional
blocks.text: The solutions of the homogeneous equation form a vector space (the kernel of L) of dimension 2. If y₁, y₂ are independent solutions, every solution is y = c₁y₁ + c₂y₂ (a fundamental set).

proof.text: The map y ↦ (y(t₀), y′(t₀)) is linear, onto ℝ² (existence) and one-to-one (uniqueness), so it is an isomorphism from the solution space to ℝ².

blocks.text: W[y₁, y₂](t) = det [y₁ y₂; y₁′ y₂′] = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂.

blocks.name: Wronskian test
blocks.text: For two solutions of the same homogeneous equation (p, q continuous on I), W is either never zero on I (independent, a fundamental set) or identically zero (dependent).

proof.text: Matching initial conditions c₁y₁(t₀) + c₂y₂(t₀) = Y₀, c₁y₁′(t₀) + c₂y₂′(t₀) = Y₁ is a 2×2 linear system with determinant W(t₀). Abel's formula W(t) = W(t₀)·e^(−∫p) shows W cannot vanish at one point without vanishing everywhere.

blocks.title: Wronskian and independence
blocks.prompt: Show e²ᵗ and e⁻ᵗ are independent solutions of y″ − y′ − 2y = 0.
steps: Both satisfy it: r² − r − 2 = (r − 2)(r + 1) has roots 2 and −1.
W = e²ᵗ·(−e⁻ᵗ) − 2e²ᵗ·e⁻ᵗ = −eᵗ − 2eᵗ = −3eᵗ ≠ 0.
blocks.answer: W = −3eᵗ ≠ 0, so they form a fundamental set: y = c₁e²ᵗ + c₂e⁻ᵗ.

blocks.text: For arbitrary functions (not solutions of one nice equation) W can vanish at some points without dependence: t and t² have W = t².

blocks.title: Wronskian of a complex-root pair
steps: y₁ = e²ᵗcos 3t, y₁′ = e²ᵗ(2cos 3t − 3sin 3t); y₂ = e²ᵗsin 3t, y₂′ = e²ᵗ(2sin 3t + 3cos 3t).
W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂ = e⁴ᵗ[cos 3t(2sin 3t + 3cos 3t) − sin 3t(2cos 3t − 3sin 3t)] = e⁴ᵗ·3(cos² + sin²) = 3e⁴ᵗ.

blocks.text: For y″ + by′ + cy = 0, Abel's formula gives W(t) = W(0)e^(−bt): here b = −4, so W = 3e⁴ᵗ is consistent. A Wronskian of two solutions is never 0 at one point and nonzero at another.

lesson.title: The characteristic equation: distinct real roots

blocks.name: Characteristic (auxiliary) equation
blocks.text: L[eʳᵗ] = (ar² + br + c)eʳᵗ. So eʳᵗ solves ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 exactly when ar² + br + c = 0.

proof.text: y = eʳᵗ gives y′ = reʳᵗ, y″ = r²eʳᵗ; factor out eʳᵗ ≠ 0.

blocks.name: Distinct real roots
blocks.text: If r₁ ≠ r₂ are real roots, y = c₁e^(r₁t) + c₂e^(r₂t).

blocks.title: Solving an IVP
items: Write the characteristic equation and find its roots.
Write the general solution (by the root case).
Plug in t₀ to both y and y′ and solve the 2×2 system for c₁, c₂.

blocks.title: Distinct real roots IVP
steps: y = c₁eᵗ + c₂e⁻³ᵗ, y′ = c₁eᵗ − 3c₂e⁻³ᵗ.
c₁ + c₂ = 0 and c₁ − 3c₂ = −4 ⇒ −4c₂ = −4 ⇒ c₂ = 1, c₁ = −1.

blocks.text: A missing y term (c = 0) means r = 0 is a root, giving the constant solution e⁰ᵗ = 1: y″ − 5y′ = 0 has y = c₁ + c₂e⁵ᵗ.

blocks.name: Repeated root
blocks.text: If r is a double root (b² − 4ac = 0, r = −b/2a), y = (c₁ + c₂t)eʳᵗ.

proof.text: Write p(r) = ar² + br + c. Differentiating L[eʳᵗ] = p(r)eʳᵗ with respect to r gives L[teʳᵗ] = (p′(r) + t·p(r))eʳᵗ. A double root has p(r) = 0 AND p′(r) = 0, so L[teʳᵗ] = 0. W[eʳᵗ, teʳᵗ] = e²ʳᵗ ≠ 0, so the two solutions are independent.

blocks.text: Why an extra t is needed: c₁eʳᵗ + c₂eʳᵗ is really one function (c₁ + c₂)eʳᵗ, so it cannot fit two initial conditions. The double root 'merges' two exponentials, and teʳᵗ is what is left of their difference quotient.

blocks.title: Repeated root IVP
steps: r² + 4r + 4 = (r + 2)²: double root −2.
y = (c₁ + c₂t)e⁻²ᵗ, y′ = c₂e⁻²ᵗ − 2(c₁ + c₂t)e⁻²ᵗ.

blocks.name: Complex roots
blocks.text: If the roots are α ± iβ (β ≠ 0), y = e^(αt)(c₁ cos βt + c₂ sin βt).

proof.text: Euler: e^((α+iβ)t) = e^(αt)(cos βt + i sin βt) is a complex solution. Since a, b, c are real, L[u + iv] = L[u] + iL[v] = 0 forces L[u] = 0 and L[v] = 0: real and imaginary parts are real solutions, and they are independent (W = βe^(2αt) ≠ 0).

blocks.title: Complex roots IVP
steps: y = eᵗ(c₁ cos 3t + c₂ sin 3t).
y(0) = c₁ = 2. y′ = eᵗ(c₁ cos 3t + c₂ sin 3t) + eᵗ(−3c₁ sin 3t + 3c₂ cos 3t), so y′(0) = c₁ + 3c₂ = −1 ⇒ c₂ = −1.

blocks.text: Do not forget the α part when differentiating: y′(0) = αc₁ + βc₂, not just βc₂.

head: Mass–spring my″ + by′ + ky = 0
Discriminant b² − 4mk
Behaviour
rows: two negative real roots, slow return

blocks.text: With m, k > 0 and b > 0 every root has negative real part, so every solution tends to 0.

blocks.title: Classify by a parameter (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Give the general solution of y″ + 4y′ + ky = 0 in each case k < 4, k = 4, k > 4. For which k do all solutions → 0?
steps: Roots r = −2 ± √(4 − k).
k < 4: distinct real r₁,₂ = −2 ± √(4 − k): y = c₁e^(r₁t) + c₂e^(r₂t).
k = 4: double root −2: y = (c₁ + c₂t)e⁻²ᵗ.
k > 4: −2 ± iβ with β = √(k − 4): y = e⁻²ᵗ(c₁cos βt + c₂sin βt).
All → 0 iff both roots have negative real part: for k < 4 need −2 + √(4 − k) < 0 ⇔ k > 0. So k > 0.
blocks.answer: Three forms as above; all solutions decay iff k > 0

blocks.title: Critical damping and an IVP
blocks.prompt: (a) m = 2, k = 8: which damping b gives critical damping? (b) Solve y″ + 2y′ + 2y = 0, y(0) = 1, y′(0) = 0.
steps: (a) Critical ⇔ b² = 4mk = 64 ⇔ b = 8.
(b) r = −1 ± i: y = e⁻ᵗ(c₁cos t + c₂sin t). y(0) = c₁ = 1; y′(0) = −c₁ + c₂ = 0 ⇒ c₂ = 1.
blocks.answer: (a) b = 8 (b) y = e⁻ᵗ(cos t + sin t)

lesson.title: Finding the equation from its solutions

blocks.title: Reverse problem
items: Each solution tells you a root: e^(rt) ↦ r; teʳᵗ ↦ r double; e^(αt)cos βt or sin βt ↦ α ± iβ.
Multiply the factors: (r − r₁)(r − r₂), or (r − α)² + β² for a complex pair.
Read off the equation from the polynomial.

blocks.title: Find the ODE
blocks.prompt: (a) Find a constant-coefficient equation with general solution c₁e²ᵗ + c₂e⁻³ᵗ. (b) One with solution e³ᵗ sin 2t. (c) Can t² solve a second-order constant-coefficient homogeneous equation?
steps: (c) Plug in: a·2 + b·2t + c·t² ≡ 0 forces a = b = c = 0. No (t² needs a triple root 0, i.e. y‴ = 0).

blocks.title: From two given solutions (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: y₁ = e²ᵗ and y₂ = e²ᵗ + e⁻ᵗ both solve ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 (constants, a = 1). Find the equation and the solution with y(0) = 0, y′(0) = 3.
steps: The solution space is a subspace: y₂ − y₁ = e⁻ᵗ is also a solution. So the roots are 2 and −1.
y = c₁e²ᵗ + c₂e⁻ᵗ: c₁ + c₂ = 0, 2c₁ − c₂ = 3 ⇒ c₁ = 1, c₂ = −1.

blocks.name: Structure
blocks.text: Every solution of L[y] = g is y = yₕ + yₚ, where yₚ is one particular solution and yₕ = c₁y₁ + c₂y₂ is the general homogeneous solution.

proof.text: If L[y] = g and L[yₚ] = g, then L[y − yₚ] = 0. Exactly like p + Nul A for Ax = b.

blocks.text: Undetermined coefficients works when the coefficients are constant and g(t) is a sum of terms tᵐe^(αt), tᵐe^(αt)cos βt, tᵐe^(αt)sin βt: derivatives of such functions stay in the same finite family, so we guess yₚ of that form with unknown coefficients.

blocks.name: The tˢ rule
blocks.text: Multiply the trial by tˢ, where s = multiplicity of α (or α + iβ) as a root of the characteristic equation: s = 0 if not a root, 1 if a simple root, 2 if a double root.

proof.text: If the trial already solves the homogeneous equation, L[trial] = 0 ≠ g and no coefficients work. Since L[teʳᵗ] = p′(r)eʳᵗ when p(r) = 0, and L[t²eʳᵗ] = p″(r)eʳᵗ when r is double, multiplying by tˢ produces a nonzero output of the right type.

blocks.text: Always include BOTH cos and sin, and the FULL polynomial of degree m, even if g has only one of them. Decide s separately for each piece of g.

blocks.title: Product forcing, no resonance
blocks.prompt: Find yₚ for y″ + y = eᵗ cos t.
steps: Roots ±i; the forcing exponent is 1 ± i, not a root ⇒ s = 0.
Trial yₚ = eᵗ(A cos t + B sin t).
Substituting gives eᵗ[(A + 2B) cos t + (B − 2A) sin t] = eᵗ cos t.

blocks.title: Product forcing with resonance: t·eᵗcos t
blocks.prompt: Find yₚ for y″ − 2y′ + 2y = t eᵗ cos t.
steps: Characteristic roots 1 ± i. The forcing has α + iβ = 1 + i, a simple root ⇒ s = 1. Polynomial degree m = 1.
Trial: yₚ = t·eᵗ[(At + B) cos t + (Ct + D) sin t].
Substituting and matching the coefficients of cos t, t cos t, sin t, t sin t gives A = 0, B = 1/4, C = 1/4, D = 0.
Check by substitution: L[(1/4)eᵗ(t cos t + t² sin t)] = t eᵗ cos t.
blocks.answer: yₚ = (1/4)eᵗ(t cos t + t² sin t)

blocks.title: Write the form only (do not solve)
blocks.prompt: Give the form of yₚ for (a) y″ − 4y′ + 4y = t e²ᵗ + e²ᵗ cos t, (b) y″ + 9y = t² sin 3t + 4e⁻ᵗ, (c) y″ + 3y′ = 5 + cos t.
steps: (a) Double root 2. t e²ᵗ: α = 2 double ⇒ s = 2: t²(At + B)e²ᵗ. e²ᵗ cos t: 2 + i not a root: e²ᵗ(C cos t + D sin t).
(b) Roots ±3i. t² sin 3t: 3i is a root, s = 1, degree 2: t[(At² + Bt + C) cos 3t + (Dt² + Et + F) sin 3t]. 4e⁻ᵗ: Ge⁻ᵗ.
(c) Roots 0, −3. Constant 5 = 5e⁰ᵗ and 0 is a root ⇒ s = 1: At. cos t: B cos t + C sin t.
blocks.answer: (a) t²(At + B)e²ᵗ + e²ᵗ(C cos t + D sin t) (b) t[(At² + Bt + C)cos 3t + (Dt² + Et + F)sin 3t] + Ge⁻ᵗ (c) At + B cos t + C sin t

blocks.title: Form for a product with resonance (exam-hard, write the form)
blocks.prompt: Write the trial form for y″ − 2y′ + 5y = t²eᵗcos 2t.
steps: Roots: r² − 2r + 5 = 0 ⇒ r = 1 ± 2i.
The forcing has α + iβ = 1 + 2i, a simple root ⇒ s = 1; polynomial degree 2.
Trial: t[(At² + Bt + C)eᵗcos 2t + (Dt² + Et + F)eᵗsin 2t]: six coefficients.
(For reference, solving gives A = C = E = 0, B = 1/16, D = 1/12, F = −1/32.)
blocks.answer: y_p = t eᵗ[(At² + Bt + C)cos 2t + (Dt² + Et + F)sin 2t]

blocks.text: Why the trial family is right: differentiating tᵐe^(αt)cos βt produces only terms tʲe^(αt)cos βt and tʲe^(αt)sin βt with j ≤ m. So L maps the finite-dimensional space spanned by these functions into itself, and undetermined coefficients is just solving a linear system in that space. Resonance means L has a kernel inside the space; multiplying by tˢ moves to a space on which L is one-to-one.

lesson.title: Superposition and full initial value problems

blocks.name: Superposition principle
blocks.text: If L[y₁] = g₁ and L[y₂] = g₂, then L[k₁y₁ + k₂y₂] = k₁g₁ + k₂g₂. So for g = g₁ + g₂, find a particular solution for each piece and add.

blocks.title: Full IVP with forcing
items: Split g into pieces; find yₚ for each (with its own tˢ).
ONLY NOW apply the initial conditions to the full y.

blocks.title: Superposition with one resonant piece
steps: yₕ = c₁ cos 2t + c₂ sin 2t (roots ±2i).
Piece 8t: trial At + B ⇒ 4At + 4B = 8t ⇒ A = 2, B = 0: yₚ₁ = 2t.
Piece 4 sin 2t: 2i is a root ⇒ s = 1, trial t(C cos 2t + D sin 2t). Substituting: −4C sin 2t + 4D cos 2t = 4 sin 2t ⇒ C = −1, D = 0: yₚ₂ = −t cos 2t.
y = c₁ cos 2t + c₂ sin 2t + 2t − t cos 2t. y(0) = c₁ = 0.
y′ = 2c₂ cos 2t + 2 − cos 2t + 2t sin 2t (with c₁ = 0); y′(0) = 2c₂ + 2 − 1 = 0 ⇒ c₂ = −1/2.
blocks.answer: y = 2t − t cos 2t − ½ sin 2t (unbounded: resonance)

blocks.text: Applying initial conditions to yₕ before adding yₚ is the most common way to lose points.
Resonance: when the forcing frequency equals a natural frequency (s = 1 with α = 0), yₚ has a factor t and the amplitude grows without bound.

blocks.title: Two forcing pieces with different tˢ (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Find the general solution of y″ − y = 2eᵗ + 3t.
steps: Roots ±1: y_h = c₁eᵗ + c₂e⁻ᵗ.
Piece 2eᵗ: 1 is a simple root ⇒ s = 1, trial Ateᵗ. With p(r) = r² − 1, L[teᵗ] = p′(1)eᵗ = 2eᵗ, so 2A = 2 ⇒ A = 1.
Piece 3t: 0 is not a root ⇒ s = 0, trial Bt + C: L[Bt + C] = 0 − (Bt + C) = 3t ⇒ B = −3, C = 0.
Add the pieces (superposition).

blocks.title: Write the form only (routine)
blocks.prompt: Give the trial form for y″ + 3y′ + 2y = t³ + e⁻ᵗ + sin t.
steps: Roots −1, −2.
t³: 0 not a root: At³ + Bt² + Ct + D.
e⁻ᵗ: −1 is a simple root: Ete⁻ᵗ.
sin t: i not a root: F cos t + G sin t.
blocks.answer: At³ + Bt² + Ct + D + Ete⁻ᵗ + F cos t + G sin t

blocks.text: A physical reading of resonance: for an undamped spring my″ + ky = F₀cos ωt, the natural frequency is ω₀ = √(k/m). If ω ≠ ω₀ the response is bounded; if ω = ω₀ the particular solution grows like t·sin ω₀t, so the amplitude increases without bound. With damping (b > 0) the homogeneous part decays and the response stays bounded for every ω.

One-line reason
rows: If y₁, y₂ solve y″ + py′ + qy = 0, so does any combination c₁y₁ + c₂y₂.
If y₁, y₂ solve L[y] = g with g ≠ 0, so does y₁ + y₂.
y = t is a solution of some ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 with constant coefficients.

It needs a triple root at 0.
If the auxiliary equation has roots 2 ± 3i, then e²ᵗcos 3t is a solution.
For y″ − 4y = e²ᵗ the trial Ae²ᵗ works.

Initial conditions may be applied to y_h before adding y_p.
Apply them to the full y = y_h + y_p.

cards.front: What does it mean for ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 to be linear, homogeneous, constant-coefficient? Why does that matter?

back.text: Meaning: Linear: y, y′, y″ appear to the first power only. Homogeneous: right side 0. Constant coefficients: a, b, c are numbers, a ≠ 0.
Why it matters: L[y] = ay″ + by′ + cy is a linear operator, so solutions are closed under addition and scaling: they form a vector space (the null space of L).
L[c₁y₁ + c₂y₂] = c₁L[y₁] + c₂L[y₂]

cards.front: Why is the solution space of ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 exactly 2-dimensional?

back.text: Why: Existence–uniqueness: for every (Y₀, Y₁) there is exactly one solution with y(0) = Y₀, y′(0) = Y₁.
So the linear map y ↦ (y(0), y′(0)) is onto (existence) and one-to-one (uniqueness): an isomorphism onto ℝ².
Consequence: Two independent solutions y₁, y₂ give every solution: y = c₁y₁ + c₂y₂.

cards.front: What is the Wronskian of y₁, y₂ and what does it tell you about solutions?

back.text: W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂
For two solutions of the same equation, W is either never 0 (independent, a fundamental set) or always 0 (dependent).
Why: Matching initial values means solving a 2×2 system whose determinant is W(t₀).
Example: e²ᵗ, e⁻³ᵗ: W = −3e⁻ᵗ − 2e⁻ᵗ = −5e⁻ᵗ ≠ 0.
For arbitrary functions W can vanish at isolated points: t and t² give W = t².

cards.front: How do you get the auxiliary (characteristic) equation and why does it work?

back.text: How: Replace y″ → r², y′ → r, y → 1: ar² + br + c = 0.
Why: L[eʳᵗ] = (ar² + br + c)eʳᵗ = p(r)eʳᵗ, and eʳᵗ ≠ 0, so eʳᵗ solves the ODE exactly when p(r) = 0.

cards.front: Three cases for the roots of ar² + br + c = 0 and the general solution in each.

items: Complex α ± iβ: e^(αt)(c₁cos βt + c₂sin βt)

back.text: Decide by: The discriminant b² − 4ac: positive, zero, negative.
For y″ + 9y = 0, r = ±3i so α = 0: c₁cos 3t + c₂sin 3t, not e³ᵗ.

cards.front: General solution of y″ − 5y′ = 0 (no y term).

back.text: r² − 5r = r(r − 5): roots 0 and 5. Since e⁰ᵗ = 1:
Example: y = c₁ + c₂e⁵ᵗ.
A missing y term means r = 0 is a root, so constants are solutions. Watch for this in the tˢ rule too.

cards.front: Why does a repeated root r give the second solution t·eʳᵗ?

back.text: Why: Differentiate L[eʳᵗ] = p(r)eʳᵗ with respect to r:
L[teʳᵗ] = (p′(r) + t·p(r))eʳᵗ
A double root has p(r) = 0 and p′(r) = 0, so L[teʳᵗ] = 0. W[eʳᵗ, teʳᵗ] = e²ʳᵗ ≠ 0, so independent.
Example: y″ − 6y′ + 9y = 0: (r − 3)², y = (c₁ + c₂t)e³ᵗ.

cards.front: Why do complex roots α ± iβ give e^(αt)cos βt and e^(αt)sin βt?

back.text: Why: Euler: e^((α+iβ)t) = e^(αt)(cos βt + i sin βt) is a complex solution. Since a, b, c are real, L[u + iv] = L[u] + iL[v] = 0 forces L[u] = 0 and L[v] = 0.
So the real part and the imaginary part are both real solutions. The conjugate root gives nothing new.
Example: y″ + 4y′ + 13y = 0: r = −2 ± 3i, y = e⁻²ᵗ(c₁cos 3t + c₂sin 3t).
β is the imaginary part only; don’t forget the e^(αt).
Example: y = eᵗ − e⁻²ᵗ.
Differentiate the general solution before plugging in t = 0.
Example: y = (1 − 2t)e²ᵗ.
Product rule on teʳᵗ: forgetting the c₂ term in y′ is the usual slip.
Example: y = 3cos 4t + 2sin 4t.
The derivative of sin 4t is 4cos 4t: the factor 4 matters.
Example: y = 2e⁻ᵗsin 2t: a decaying oscillation.

cards.front: Mass–spring my″ + by′ + ky = 0: what do under-, critically and overdamped mean?

back.text: discriminant b² − 4mk

items: = 0 critical: repeated root, fastest return without oscillating.
> 0 overdamped: two negative real roots, slow return.

back.text: Example: y″ + 6y′ + 5y = 0: roots −1, −5, overdamped.
With b > 0 all roots have negative real part, so every solution → 0.

cards.front: Find a constant-coefficient ODE with solution e⁻ᵗcos 4t. Can t² solve a 2nd-order one?

back.text: t²?: No: t² needs a triple root at 0, i.e. y‴ = 0, which is 3rd order.
Lowest order = total number of roots needed (counting multiplicity).

cards.front: Structure of the solutions of ay″ + by′ + cy = g(t)?

back.text: y = yₕ + yₚ = c₁y₁ + c₂y₂ + yₚ
Why: If y and yₚ both solve L[y] = g, then L[y − yₚ] = 0, so y − yₚ is a homogeneous solution.
Same as Ax = b: one particular solution + the null space.
Solutions of L[y] = g are not a subspace: the sum of two solves L[y] = 2g.

cards.front: State the superposition principle and how it’s used.

back.text: L[y₁] = g₁, L[y₂] = g₂ ⟹ L[k₁y₁ + k₂y₂] = k₁g₁ + k₂g₂
Use: For a forcing that’s a sum, find a particular solution for each piece separately, scale, and add.
Example: If t solves L[y] = 3 and eᵗ solves L[y] = 2eᵗ, then 2t − ½eᵗ solves L[y] = 6 − eᵗ.

cards.front: What is the idea of undetermined coefficients, and when does it apply?

back.text: Idea: Derivatives of polynomials, exponentials and sin/cos stay in the same family, so guess yₚ of the same type as g with unknown coefficients, substitute, match coefficients.
Applies when: Constant coefficients and g is a sum of products of polynomials, e^(αt), cos βt, sin βt.
Not for g = tan t, 1/t, ln t.

cards.front: How do you choose the trial form? (The table is given on the exam; how do you use it?)

back.title: Steps
items: Solve the homogeneous equation first (you need the roots).
Read off α (or α + iβ) and the polynomial degree n of g.
Write a full degree-n polynomial, and both cos and sin.
Multiply by tˢ, s = multiplicity of α (or α + iβ) as a root: 0, 1 or 2.

back.text: Example: g = t²: try At² + Bt + C (not just At²).
A cos t alone fails when there’s a y′ term.

cards.front: Find yₚ for y″ − y′ − 2y = 4t².

back.title: Steps
items: Roots 2, −1; 0 is not a root, s = 0.
Try At² + Bt + C: 2A − (2At + B) − 2(At² + Bt + C) = 4t².

back.text: Example: yₚ = −2t² + 2t − 3.

cards.front: Find yₚ for y″ + 2y′ + 5y = 10cos t.

back.title: Steps
items: Roots −1 ± 2i; i is not a root, s = 0.
Try A cos t + B sin t. Substituting: (4A + 2B)cos t + (4B − 2A)sin t = 10cos t.

back.text: Example: yₚ = 2cos t + sin t.
Include sin even though g has only cos.

cards.front: Why multiply the trial by t when it solves the homogeneous equation?

back.text: Why: If the trial is a homogeneous solution, L[trial] = 0 ≠ g: no coefficients can work.
L[teʳᵗ] = (p′(r) + t·p(r))eʳᵗ
Simple root: p(r) = 0, p′(r) ≠ 0, so L[Ateʳᵗ] = A·p′(r)eʳᵗ: solvable. Double root needs t²: L[t²eʳᵗ] = p″(r)eʳᵗ.
Example: y″ − y′ − 2y = 6e²ᵗ: p′(2) = 3, so 3A = 6, yₚ = 2te²ᵗ.

cards.front: Find yₚ for y″ + 4y = 12cos 2t. What is this phenomenon?

back.title: Steps
items: Roots ±2i, and 2i is a root: s = 1.
Try t(A cos 2t + B sin 2t). Substituting gives −4A sin 2t + 4B cos 2t = 12cos 2t.

back.text: Example: yₚ = 3t sin 2t: resonance, the amplitude grows without bound.
Plain A cos 2t + B sin 2t gives 0.

cards.front: Quick yₚ: (a) y″ − 3y′ + 2y = 4; (b) y″ − 3y′ + 2y = eᵗ; (c) y″ − 6y′ + 9y = e³ᵗ.

back.title: Steps
items: (b) roots 1, 2; 1 is simple: Ateᵗ, A·p′(1) = A(2 − 3) = 1 → yₚ = −teᵗ.

cards.front: Trial form (don’t solve) for y″ − 4y′ + 4y = te²ᵗ + e²ᵗcos t.

back.title: Steps
items: te²ᵗ: degree 1, α = 2 double root, s = 2 → t²(At + B)e²ᵗ.
e²ᵗcos t: 2 + i not a root, s = 0 → e²ᵗ(C cos t + D sin t).

back.text: Example: yₚ = t²(At + B)e²ᵗ + e²ᵗ(C cos t + D sin t).
Decide s for each piece separately; multiply the whole block: t²(At + B), not At³ + B.

cards.front: Trial form (don’t solve) for y″ + 9y = t²sin 3t + 4e⁻ᵗ.

back.title: Steps
items: 3i is a root (s = 1), polynomial degree 2: t[(At² + Bt + C)cos 3t + (Dt² + Et + F)sin 3t].

back.text: Full degree-2 polynomials on both cos and sin, even though g has only sin.

cards.front: Solve y″ + y = 2t, y(0) = 0, y′(0) = 0. In what order do you do things?

back.title: Steps
items: y = c₁cos t + c₂sin t + 2t, then initial conditions: c₁ = 0, c₂ + 2 = 0.

back.text: Example: y = 2t − 2sin t.
Apply initial conditions to yₕ + yₚ, never to yₕ alone.

cards.front: Why does a repeated root r give both eʳᵗ and teʳᵗ?

back.text: L[teʳᵗ] = (p′(r) + t p(r))eʳᵗ, and a double root has p(r) = p′(r) = 0. One exponential alone can't meet two initial conditions.

cards.front: When does the undetermined-coefficients guess need an extra factor of t, and why?

back.text: When the trial (its exponent α or α + iβ) is a root of the characteristic equation: then L[trial] = 0 and cannot equal g. Multiply by tˢ, s = multiplicity of the root.

cards.front: Undetermined coefficients for y″ + y′ = 3?

back.text: 0 is a root (no y term), so try At: A = 3, yₚ = 3t.

solution.text: What it tests: Differentiate the product correctly: y′(0) picks up −2c₁ from the exponential. Forgetting it gives c₂ = 0.

hard.title: Repeated root IVP: zero and maximum

prompt.text: Solve y″ − 6y′ + 9y = 0, y(0) = 2, y′(0) = 1. At what t > 0 does y vanish, and where is its maximum?

hard.answer: y = (2 − 5t)e³ᵗ; zero at t = 2/5; maximum at t = 1/15

solution.text: What it tests: Repeated root needs the extra t: c₁e3t + c₂e3t is only one function.

prompt.text: Solve y″ + 9y = 6 cos 3t, y(0) = 0, y′(0) = 0. Is the solution bounded?

solution.title: Solution
items: Homogeneous: r = ±3i: cos 3t, sin 3t. The forcing frequency matches ⇒ multiply the trial by t: yₚ = t(A cos 3t + B sin 3t).

solution.text: What it tests: Trial A cos 3t + B sin 3t without t gives 0 = 6 cos 3t. Shortcut for y″ + ω²y: L[t sin ωt] = 2ω cos ωt.

hard.title: Trial forms only

prompt.text: Write the form of a particular solution (do not solve for coefficients):

hard.answer: (a) t²(At + B)e²ᵗ + e²ᵗ(C cos t + D sin t) + Et² + Ft + G + H cos 2t + K sin 2t (b) te⁻ᵗ(A cos 2t + B sin 2t) + (Ct + D)e⁻ᵗ

solution.title: Solution
items: te2t: 2 is a double root ⇒ multiply by t²: t²(At + B)e2t.
e2t sin t: 2 ± i not roots: e2t(C cos t + D sin t). 3t²: Et² + Ft + G. cos 2t: ±2i not roots: H cos 2t + K sin 2t.
(b) Roots −1 ± 2i. e−t sin 2t matches a root ⇒ te−t(A cos 2t + B sin 2t). te−t: −1 is not a root ⇒ (Ct + D)e−t.
(For reference, solving gives (a) yₚ = t³e2t/6 − e2t sin t + (3/4)t² + (3/2)t + 9/8 − (1/8) sin 2t; (b) yₚ = −(1/4)te−t cos 2t + (1/4)te−t.)

solution.text: What it tests: Multiplier = ts where s = multiplicity of the exponent (α or α ± βi) as a root. A polynomial of degree m on the right needs a full degree-m polynomial (all lower terms) in the trial.

solution.title: Solution
items: For −2e−t: −1 is a simple root ⇒ Cte−t. With p(r) = r² − r − 2, L[tert] = p′(r)ert when p(r) = 0; p′(−1) = −3 ⇒ −3C = −2 ⇒ C = 2/3.

solution.text: What it tests: Handle each forcing term separately, then add. The −2e−t piece is resonant; the 4t piece is not.

4. The Wronskian of two solutions of y″ + p(t)y′ + q(t)y = 0 (p, q continuous on I) is either identically zero on I or never zero on I.
5. et cos t and et sin t are solutions of y″ − 2y′ + 2y = 0.

hard.title: Reverse-engineer an ODE and its forcing

prompt.text: (a) Find a constant-coefficient homogeneous equation having y = e2t(3 cos t − sin t) as a solution. (b) Find g(t) so that y = t sin 2t solves y″ + 4y = g(t), and give the general solution of that equation.

hard.answer: (a) y″ − 4y′ + 5y = 0 (b) g = 4 cos 2t; y = c₁ cos 2t + c₂ sin 2t + t sin 2t

solution.text: What it tests: Reverse engineering: from solution to roots to characteristic polynomial. Just plug y in to find g.

hard.title: Parameter analysis: decay, oscillation, boundedness

prompt.text: (a) For which k do all solutions of y″ + ky′ + 4y = 0 tend to 0? For which do nonzero solutions oscillate (cross zero infinitely often)? (b) For which real k does y″ + ky = cos 2t have at least one unbounded solution?

hard.answer: (a) all → 0 iff k > 0; oscillate iff |k| < 4 (b) k = 4 or k ≤ 0

solution.title: Solution
items: (a) Roots (−k ± √(k² − 16))/2. Real parts all negative ⇔ k > 0 (product of roots is 4 > 0, sum is −k). k = 0: pure oscillation, no decay. k < 0: growth.
k = 0: y = c₁ + c₂t − cos 2t/4 — unbounded when c₂ ≠ 0. k < 0: e√(−k)t appears. Answer: k = 4 or k ≤ 0.

solution.text: What it tests: Everyone finds k = 4. Exam-proof answers also check when the homogeneous part itself blows up.

prompt.text: (a) Show y₁ = et, y₂ = tet are linearly independent on ℝ and find the constant-coefficient equation they solve. (b) Can y₁ = t and y₂ = |t| both be solutions on (−1, 1) of some y″ + p(t)y′ + q(t)y = 0 with continuous p, q?

solution.text: (b) |t| is not differentiable at 0, so it can’t be a C² solution: no. (Even ignoring that: on (0,1) they coincide and their Wronskian is 0 there, but they’re independent on (−1,1) — impossible for genuine solutions by Abel’s theorem.)
What it tests: Nonzero Wronskian at one point ⇒ independent. For solutions of a nice ODE, zero Wronskian anywhere ⇒ dependent; for arbitrary functions that implication fails.

hard.title: Full IVP with a double-root resonance

solution.title: Solution
items: et: 1 is a double root ⇒ At²et. Plugging in, everything cancels except 2Aet ⇒ A = 1/2.

solution.text: What it tests: Apply initial conditions to the full solution (yₕ + yₚ), never to yₕ alone. Double root ⇒ t² multiplier.

keyFacts: ar² + br + c = 0: distinct real → c₁e^(r₁t) + c₂e^(r₂t); double → (c₁ + c₂t)eʳᵗ; α ± iβ → e^(αt)(c₁cos βt + c₂sin βt).
Solution space of the homogeneous equation is 2-dimensional; W = y₁y₂′ − y₁′y₂ ≠ 0 ⇔ fundamental set.
General solution of L[y] = g: y = yₕ + yₚ; apply initial conditions to the full y.
Trial: full polynomial of degree m, both cos and sin, times tˢ (s = multiplicity of α or α + iβ as a root).
L[teʳᵗ] = p′(r)eʳᵗ when p(r) = 0; L[t²eʳᵗ] = p″(r)eʳᵗ for a double root.
Superposition: split g into pieces, solve each, add.
Damping b² − 4mk: < 0 under, = 0 critical, > 0 over; resonance when forcing matches ±iω.

parsons.title: Solve an IVP step by step
lines: Initial conditions: c₁ + c₂ = 1 and c₁ + 2c₂ = 0.
distractors: Initial conditions: c₁ + c₂ = 1 and c₁ − 2c₂ = 0.

parsons.title: Why a double root gives teʳᵗ
parsons.goal: Let p(r) = ar² + br + c have a double root r₀. Prove that y = te^(r₀t) solves ay″ + by′ + cy = 0.
lines: For y = teʳᵗ: y′ = eʳᵗ + rteʳᵗ and y″ = 2reʳᵗ + r²teʳᵗ.
Substitute: ay″ + by′ + cy = eʳᵗ[t(ar² + br + c) + (2ar + b)].
A double root satisfies p(r₀) = 0 and p′(r₀) = 2ar₀ + b = 0.
So L[te^(r₀t)] = 0: te^(r₀t) is a solution. ∎
distractors: For y = teʳᵗ: y′ = rteʳᵗ and y″ = r²teʳᵗ.
A double root satisfies p(r₀) = 0 and p″(r₀) = 0.

parsons.title: Superposition principle
parsons.goal: Prove: if L[y₁] = g₁ and L[y₂] = g₂ for L[y] = ay″ + by′ + cy, then L[k₁y₁ + k₂y₂] = k₁g₁ + k₂g₂.
lines: Let y = k₁y₁ + k₂y₂. Then y′ = k₁y₁′ + k₂y₂′ and y″ = k₁y₁″ + k₂y₂″.
L[y] = a(k₁y₁″ + k₂y₂″) + b(k₁y₁′ + k₂y₂′) + c(k₁y₁ + k₂y₂).
Regroup: L[y] = k₁(ay₁″ + by₁′ + cy₁) + k₂(ay₂″ + by₂′ + cy₂).
This is k₁L[y₁] + k₂L[y₂] = k₁g₁ + k₂g₂. ∎
distractors: Since L is nonlinear, regrouping is not allowed.
